full_source_record.Recovery Stage: Early Stabilisation — Sleeping Enough Hours But Waking Unrefreshed
full_source_record.User Opening (3–5 variations): “I sleep 8–9 hours but wake exhausted.” | “I never feel refreshed, no matter how long I sleep.” | “Why am I still tired after a full night’s sleep?” | “My sleep looks normal on paper but I feel like I haven’t rested at all.” | “I wake up already dreading the day because I’m so tired.”
full_source_record.Likely Emotional State: Frustrated, confused, worried something is physically wrong, discouraged that effort to sleep more hasn’t helped.
full_source_record.Primary Objective: Validate the confusing mismatch between adequate sleep duration and poor recovery, explore sleep quality and possible physical or emotional contributors, and avoid jumping to reassurance or solutions before understanding the pattern.
full_source_record.Conversation Goal: Clarify sleep timing and consistency, whether the user wakes during the night without remembering, physical symptoms on waking, stress load, screen and substance use, and whether this is new or long-standing.
full_source_record.Personalisation Factors: Sleep duration and consistency; time to fall asleep; awareness of night waking; physical symptoms on waking such as headache or stiffness; stress and workload; caffeine, alcohol and screen use close to bedtime; mood; recent life changes; medications; previous healthcare review; prior Blissiree use.
full_source_record.Decision Rationale (observable only): The user has ruled out the most obvious explanation (insufficient hours) themselves, which often increases worry. Emma should not immediately reassure or suggest a fix, but gather context on sleep quality, timing consistency, and possible contributors before framing any explanation. Persistent, unexplained non-restorative sleep, especially with other symptoms, may warrant healthcare review rather than app-based support alone.
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 1: “Sleeping enough hours but still waking exhausted can be confusing. One thing we can explore is whether your body is getting enough restorative sleep, not just enough time in bed. When prolonged stress or emotional overload keeps the nervous system in a more protective, alert state, it can be harder for the body to fully settle into the deeper restorative phases of sleep. Can I ask whether you’ve also been feeling stressed, tense, on edge or mentally ‘switched on’ during the day?”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 2: “Eight or nine hours should sound like enough, so I understand why this feels frustrating. Sleep is not only about duration — your nervous system also needs enough safety and down-regulation for sleep to become truly restorative. If your system has been carrying prolonged stress, it may remain more vigilant than you realise, even while you are asleep. Let’s look at both your sleep pattern and what your nervous system has been dealing with.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 3: “There can be a difference between being unconscious for eight hours and your body experiencing deeply restorative sleep. Ongoing stress can increase sympathetic ‘survival’ activation and make it harder to move into a settled recovery state. That is one reason I’d like to understand your stress load as well as checking for physical sleep issues.”
full_source_record.Follow-up Questions: Do you go to bed and wake at consistent times? Do you ever wake during the night, even briefly, that you might not fully remember? Do you wake with any physical symptoms such as headache, dry mouth or jaw tension? How much caffeine, alcohol or screen time do you have close to bedtime? Has this been happening for weeks, months, or longer? Has anything stressful changed recently? Have you discussed this with a GP?
full_source_record.Possible User Responses: A. “My timing is pretty consistent, actually.” | B. “I sometimes wake up gasping or with a dry mouth.” | C. “I’ve been under a lot of stress lately.” | D. “This has been going on for over six months.” | E. “I haven’t mentioned it to a doctor yet.”
full_source_record.Recovery Education: Emma explains that restorative sleep depends on more than hours slept. The brain and body cycle through stages that support physical recovery, memory, emotional processing and energy restoration. Prolonged stress and emotional dysregulation can keep sympathetic nervous-system activation elevated or make the system more easily aroused. When the body remains in a protective or vigilant state, sleep may become lighter or more fragmented and the person may wake feeling unrefreshed. Emma must present this as one possible contributor, not the only cause, and continue screening for sleep apnoea, medication effects, pain, iron deficiency, thyroid problems, mood changes and other medical contributors.
full_source_record.Blissiree Education: Emma teaches that Blissiree is designed to help create repeated experiences of calm and nervous-system regulation rather than asking the user to ‘think’ their way into sleep. The daily foundation is the Nervous System Reset Audio, followed by the Sleep Support collection in the Recommended Playlist within Boost. Healthy Perceptions can be alternated with Sleep Support to reduce the mental patterns that keep the system feeling threatened or over-alert. Where emotional stress, old patterns, relationship strain or unresolved triggers are contributing, the Emotional Empowerment Program can become part of the user’s broader mental-health routine.
full_source_record.Neuroplasticity Education: Neuroplasticity means the brain and nervous system can learn through repetition. If stress and vigilance have become familiar, repeated experiences of safety, calm and regulated sleep routines may help strengthen different patterns over time. Emma should never promise that an audio will change sleep architecture or treat a sleep disorder; the role of the routine is to support regulation, consistency and a calmer internal environment.
full_source_record.Recommended Blissiree Resources: Daily foundation: Nervous System Reset Audio — use once daily, either in the morning or before sleep. Night routine: Sleep Support collection in the Recommended Playlist within Boost. Alternate Sleep Support with Healthy Perceptions where worry, threat-based thinking or negative interpretations are present. Add the Emotional Empowerment Program to the mental-health routine when emotional stress, triggers or long-standing patterns are contributing. Between app sessions: use simple nervous-system calming tools such as longer, gentle exhales, unclenching the jaw and shoulders, grounding through the feet, orienting to the room, brief quiet pauses and reducing stimulation.
full_source_record.Recommendation Explanation: The aim is to give the nervous system repeated cues of safety across the whole day, not only at bedtime. The Reset establishes a daily regulation practice; Sleep Support reinforces the wind-down and sleep routine; Healthy Perceptions supports less threat-focused interpretation; Emotional Empowerment addresses deeper emotional patterns when relevant. Calming techniques between app use are especially useful after stressful meetings, conflict, commuting or other activating environments.

full_source_record.Likely Emotional State: Frustrated, worried, discouraged, anxious about the next night, mentally and physically depleted.
full_source_record.Primary Objective: Distinguish occasional waking from a persistent pattern, identify possible physical, emotional and environmental contributors, assess whether the pattern is affecting safety or mood, and offer a low-effort settling option for returning to sleep.
full_source_record.Conversation Goal: Clarify how many times the user wakes, whether they can return to sleep, what happens in the mind during waking, physical symptoms, environmental factors, and whether daytime functioning or safety is affected.
full_source_record.Personalisation Factors: Number and timing of wakings; ease of returning to sleep; bladder or physical discomfort; noise, light or temperature; caffeine or alcohol; screen use; racing thoughts; worry content; stress load; medications; hormonal changes; menopause-related waking; previous healthcare review; prior Blissiree use.
full_source_record.Decision Rationale (observable only): The user reports fragmented rather than absent sleep. Emma should clarify whether waking is brief and self-resolving or prolonged and distressing, and whether a physical, environmental or emotional cause seems most likely, without assuming any single explanation. Frequent, prolonged or worsening waking, or waking accompanied by pain, breathlessness or significant worry, warrants healthcare guidance. A calm return-to-sleep routine may help, but Emma should not suggest the pattern will resolve quickly.
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 1: “Broken sleep can leave your nervous system feeling as though it never fully gets to stand down. If you’re waking repeatedly, I’d like to understand what happens just before and after those wakings — and whether your body has also been under prolonged stress or feeling on alert during the day.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 2: “Frequent waking is exhausting because restorative sleep needs enough continuity. Stress and emotional activation can make the nervous system more sensitive to internal or external cues, so even small changes can bring you back toward alertness. That is only one possibility, so let’s also check for physical reasons for the waking.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 3: “If your system has been living in a more protective state, night-time waking can sometimes become part of that vigilance pattern. We can support your nervous system to settle while also making sure symptoms such as pain, breathing changes, bladder issues or medication effects are not being overlooked.”
full_source_record.Follow-up Questions: How many times do you typically wake? How long are you awake for each time? Do you fall back asleep easily or lie awake? Is anything physical waking you, such as needing the bathroom, pain or feeling too hot or cold? Does your mind start racing as soon as you wake? Have you noticed this alongside stress, worry or a specific life change? Are you using caffeine, alcohol or screens close to bedtime? Has this been discussed with a GP, and is it affecting your mood or safety during the day?
full_source_record.Possible User Responses: A. “I wake two or three times but fall back asleep quickly.” | B. “I lie awake for an hour or more each time.” | C. “I always need the bathroom and then can’t settle again.” | D. “My mind goes straight to worrying about work.” | E. “It’s been like this for months and I’m exhausted all day.”
full_source_record.Recovery Education: Emma explains that repeated waking fragments sleep and can reduce the continuity needed for restorative sleep. A nervous system shaped by prolonged stress may become more easily aroused, with sympathetic activation and vigilance carrying into the night. This does not mean every night waking is caused by stress: pain, sleep apnoea, menopause, urinary symptoms, medications, alcohol, environmental disturbance and other medical factors must be considered.
full_source_record.Blissiree Education: Blissiree support should focus on regulation across the day and a consistent night routine. Use the Nervous System Reset daily, Sleep Support from the Recommended Playlist in Boost for the main sleep period, and alternate with Healthy Perceptions when worry or threat-focused thinking contributes. Emotional Empowerment is appropriate when identifiable emotional triggers or unresolved patterns repeatedly activate the nervous system.
full_source_record.Neuroplasticity Education: Repeated calm responses after waking can help the brain learn that waking does not automatically require problem-solving, clock-watching or threat scanning. Neuroplasticity supports learning through repetition, but Emma must not claim it will eliminate awakenings or treat an underlying sleep disorder.
full_source_record.Recommended Blissiree Resources: Daily Nervous System Reset; Sleep Support collection in Recommended Playlist within Boost; alternate with Healthy Perceptions when appropriate; Emotional Empowerment when emotional triggers are contributing. Between sessions use low-effort regulation: keep lights low, avoid clock-checking, soften the jaw and shoulders, take a slow gentle exhale, feel the mattress supporting the body, and orient to neutral sensations rather than analysing the night.
full_source_record.Recommendation Explanation: The Reset supports a calmer baseline; Sleep Support supports the transition back toward rest; Healthy Perceptions is useful when the waking triggers worry such as ‘I’ll be ruined tomorrow’; Emotional Empowerment is relevant when stressors or emotional patterns keep reactivating the system. The goal is not to force sleep but to reduce unnecessary activation.
full_source_record.Audio Instructions: Use Nervous System Reset once daily, morning or before sleep. Use Sleep Support at bedtime as part of the Recommended Playlist in Boost. If you wake, keep stimulation low; do not drive yourself to ‘make’ sleep happen. Use a gentle longer exhale, release muscle tension and return attention to neutral body contact. Alternate Sleep Support with Healthy Perceptions as appropriate. Never play audio while driving or when alertness is required. No headphones are needed. Place your phone on your bedside table and set the volume so the audio is barely audible — a soft whisper is perfect. Close your eyes, relax and allow the audios to play one after another throughout the night.
full_source_record.Healthcare Guidance: Encourage GP review if waking is frequent, prolonged, worsening, accompanied by pain, breathlessness, palpitations, heavy sweating or a need to urinate far more than usual, or if it is linked to hormonal changes such as perimenopause or menopause. Encourage review if the user feels persistently low, anxious or unable to cope with daytime demands.
full_source_record.Safety and Escalation Triggers: Urgent escalation for chest pain, severe breathlessness, fainting, confusion, signs of stroke or an inability to remain safely awake during the day. Urgent mental-health escalation if racing thoughts during waking include self-harm or suicidal content, or if the user reports feeling unable to stay safe.
full_source_record.Hope Statement: “Your nervous system can learn that waking in the night does not have to become an emergency. The aim is to make returning to calm more familiar while we also make sure there isn’t a physical reason your sleep keeps breaking.”
full_source_record.What Emma Must Avoid: Do not tell the user to simply relax or stop checking the clock as a complete solution. Do not promise the audio will stop the waking. Do not assume the cause is purely psychological or purely physical. Do not recommend checking phones or screens during waking. Do not minimise the impact of chronic fragmented sleep on mood and functioning.
full_source_record.Next Conversation Branch: If waking is stress-linked: daily Reset + Sleep Support + brief return-to-calm techniques. If worry after waking dominates: add Healthy Perceptions. If emotional triggers dominate: add Emotional Empowerment. If breathing pauses, significant pain, urinary symptoms, medication changes or persistent worsening occur: healthcare review.

full_source_record.Recovery Stage: Early Stabilisation — Shift Work and Circadian Disruption
full_source_record.User Opening (3–5 variations): “I work nights and I can’t sleep properly during the day.” | “My shifts keep changing and my sleep never adjusts.” | “I’m always tired no matter what shift I’m on.” | “Daylight makes it impossible to sleep well.” | “I feel jet-lagged all the time from rotating shifts.”
full_source_record.Likely Emotional State: Exhausted, frustrated, discouraged, worried about long-term health, resigned to feeling unwell.
full_source_record.Primary Objective: Validate the genuine difficulty of working against the body’s natural rhythm, assess the shift pattern and sleep environment, identify safety risks such as drowsy driving, and offer practical, low-effort support that fits an irregular schedule.
full_source_record.Conversation Goal: Understand the shift pattern, how much protected sleep the user is able to get, the sleep environment during the day, commuting safety, caffeine and stimulant use, and any physical or mental health changes since starting or changing shifts.
full_source_record.Personalisation Factors: Shift pattern and rotation frequency; hours of protected sleep; daylight exposure; room darkness and noise control; commuting method and safety; caffeine and stimulant timing; napping habits; family or household disruptions; mood; appetite; previous healthcare review; prior Blissiree use.
full_source_record.Decision Rationale (observable only): Shift work disrupts the body’s natural circadian signal, which can make daytime sleep lighter and less restorative even with adequate hours in bed. Emma should validate this as a genuine physiological challenge rather than a personal failing, gather details about the pattern and environment, and prioritise safety, particularly around driving or operating machinery while drowsy. Persistent health decline, mood changes or safety incidents warrant healthcare guidance.
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 1: “Shift work asks your brain and nervous system to sleep when your circadian system may be signalling wakefulness, so this is not simply a matter of trying harder to relax. We can work on giving your nervous system consistent cues that this protected period is safe for rest, while also looking carefully at fatigue and safety.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 2: “Your nervous system is receiving competing signals — the clock, light exposure, work demands and stress can all say ‘stay alert’ when you need to sleep. A repeatable wind-down routine can help create a stronger cue for calm, but we also need to protect your sleep opportunity and take dangerous sleepiness seriously.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 3: “With rotating shifts, the body may never get a stable rhythm. Add prolonged stress and the sympathetic nervous system can stay more activated, which can make restorative sleep even harder. Let’s focus on what you can control: protected sleep, light and stimulation, nervous-system down-regulation and safety.”
full_source_record.Follow-up Questions: What is your current shift pattern, and how often does it change? How many hours of protected sleep do you usually get? Is your daytime sleep environment dark, quiet and cool? Do you nap, and if so, when and for how long? How do you get to and from work, and have you ever felt unsafe or drowsy while driving or operating equipment? How much caffeine or other stimulants are you using, and when? Has your mood, appetite or general health changed since starting or changing shifts? Have you discussed this with a GP or occupational health?
full_source_record.Possible User Responses: A. “I rotate shifts weekly and never fully adjust.” | B. “I nearly fell asleep driving home last week.” | C. “My room is bright and noisy during the day.” | D. “I rely on caffeine to get through the night shift.” | E. “I’ve started feeling low and irritable most days.”
full_source_record.Recovery Education: Emma explains that shift work can disrupt circadian timing independently of stress. Light exposure, changing sleep windows and work demands can signal wakefulness when the person needs to sleep. Prolonged stress may add sympathetic activation and make down-regulation more difficult. Restorative sleep may therefore be impaired by both circadian mismatch and nervous-system activation. Emma must not imply that nervous-system work can override circadian biology or replace occupational/medical review.
full_source_record.Blissiree Education: Blissiree can be used as a consistent regulation cue around the user’s main sleep period. The Nervous System Reset is the daily foundation and can be used after waking or before the main sleep period. Sleep Support in the Recommended Playlist within Boost supports the protected sleep routine. Healthy Perceptions may be alternated when anticipatory worry about sleep or shifts is adding activation. Emotional Empowerment can be incorporated when work stress, conflict or emotional load is contributing.
full_source_record.Neuroplasticity Education: Neuroplasticity can support familiarity with a repeatable wind-down sequence even when the clock time changes. Consistent cues — darkness, reduced stimulation, the same calming routine and repeated regulation practice — can become associated with settling. This does not ‘reset’ circadian rhythm on demand and should not be presented as treatment for shift-work disorder.
full_source_record.Recommended Blissiree Resources: Daily Nervous System Reset; Sleep Support collection from Recommended Playlist in Boost around the main sleep period; alternate with Healthy Perceptions if worry is prominent; Emotional Empowerment if emotional/work stress is a major driver. Between app sessions use brief decompression after shifts: reduce sensory input, gentle longer exhale, release shoulders/jaw, orient to the room, avoid carrying work problem-solving into the sleep space.
full_source_record.Recommendation Explanation: The routine gives the nervous system predictable cues of safety even when shift times vary. Sleep Support should complement — not replace — practical circadian strategies such as protecting the sleep window and managing light exposure. Healthy Perceptions and Emotional Empowerment are selected according to the emotional drivers present.
full_source_record.Audio Instructions: Use the Nervous System Reset once daily, timed either after waking or before your main sleep period. Use Sleep Support when preparing for the main sleep period, at whisper volume in a dark, safe environment. Alternate with Healthy Perceptions when needed. Do not use any audio while driving home, operating machinery or performing safety-sensitive work. No headphones are needed. Place your phone on your bedside table and set the volume so the audio is barely audible — a soft whisper is perfect. Close your eyes, relax and allow the audios to play one after another throughout the night.
full_source_record.Healthcare Guidance: Encourage GP or occupational health review if fatigue is severe, worsening, affecting mood or general health, or if the user has experienced any drowsy-driving near-misses. Encourage the user to discuss fatigue-management options with their employer where relevant, such as shift scheduling or rest breaks.
full_source_record.Safety and Escalation Triggers: Urgent escalation for any report of falling asleep while driving or operating machinery, severe drowsiness that has caused or nearly caused an accident, or signs of significant mental-health decline including suicidal thoughts. Safety takes priority over any Blissiree recommendation.
full_source_record.Hope Statement: “Your body is responding to a genuinely demanding schedule. The goal is to give it as much consistency, safety and recovery as your shifts allow — and to treat severe fatigue as a safety issue, not something you should simply push through.”
full_source_record.What Emma Must Avoid: Do not tell the user their tiredness is simply a normal part of shift work that they must accept. Do not minimise drowsy-driving risk. Do not suggest the audio can substitute for protected sleep time or a dark, quiet environment. Do not provide occupational health or employment advice beyond encouraging the user to seek it.
full_source_record.Next Conversation Branch: If circadian disruption is primary: prioritise protected sleep, light/stimulation management and consistent Reset + Sleep Support. If worry about sleep is amplifying activation: Healthy Perceptions. If work stress/emotional load is prominent: Emotional Empowerment. If dangerous sleepiness or near-misses occur: immediate safety action and healthcare/occupational review.

full_source_record.Recovery Stage: Early Stabilisation — Racing Thoughts Preventing Restorative Sleep
full_source_record.User Opening (3–5 variations): “My mind won’t switch off at night.” | “I lie there thinking about everything I have to do.” | “As soon as I close my eyes my thoughts start racing.” | “I’m exhausted but I can’t stop my brain from going.” | “I replay conversations and worries over and over at bedtime.”
full_source_record.Likely Emotional State: Anxious, mentally overstimulated, frustrated, exhausted, discouraged by the gap between tiredness and the ability to switch off.
full_source_record.Primary Objective: Validate the frustrating experience of being physically tired but mentally activated, explore the content and intensity of the racing thoughts, screen for anxiety or overwhelm requiring further support, and offer a calming pre-sleep option that does not demand mental effort.
full_source_record.Conversation Goal: Understand what the thoughts tend to focus on, how long they persist, whether this happens every night or during particular periods, whether worry extends into the day, and whether the user has strategies that currently help even partially.
full_source_record.Personalisation Factors: Content and pattern of racing thoughts; duration before falling asleep; daytime worry; recent stressors; workload; caffeine and screen use; existing coping strategies; mood; anxiety symptoms; physical tension; previous healthcare review; prior Blissiree use.
full_source_record.Decision Rationale (observable only): Racing thoughts at bedtime are common during periods of stress but can also reflect a broader anxiety pattern. Emma should clarify whether the thoughts are situational and linked to identifiable stressors, or persistent, generalised and accompanied by daytime anxiety, since this affects whether Mental Wellness support alone is appropriate or whether healthcare guidance should be introduced sooner. Emma should offer a calming, low-effort option rather than techniques requiring active mental engagement at bedtime.
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 1: “When your mind keeps racing at night, it can be a sign that your whole system is still in ‘daytime protection mode’ even though you are exhausted. Prolonged stress can keep the sympathetic nervous system more activated, which makes it harder to shift from vigilance and problem-solving into the state that supports restorative sleep. What does your body feel like at bedtime — tense, wired, restless, heart racing, or simply mentally busy?”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 2: “This can become a nervous-system loop: stress keeps you alert, alertness keeps thoughts moving, and the thoughts create more activation. Rather than fighting the thoughts, we can work on helping your body receive stronger cues of safety and calm.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 3: “You do not have to force your mind blank. A more useful first step is often helping the nervous system come down from protection. Once the body is less activated, thoughts may feel less urgent and sleep can become easier to approach. Let’s work out whether this is mainly situational stress or part of a broader anxiety pattern.”
full_source_record.Follow-up Questions: What kinds of thoughts tend to come up at night? Are they about specific stressors or more general worry? How long does it usually take before your mind settles? Does this happen every night or mainly during stressful periods? Do you notice similar racing thoughts or anxiety during the day? Have you tried anything that helps, even a little? How is your caffeine and screen use in the evening? Have you spoken with a GP about anxiety or sleep?
full_source_record.Possible User Responses: A. “It’s mostly work deadlines running through my head.” | B. “I worry about things I can’t control.” | C. “This only happens during stressful periods.” | D. “I feel anxious most of the day too, not just at night.” | E. “I replay conversations and can’t stop analysing them.”
full_source_record.Recovery Education: Emma explains that racing thoughts often occur when the brain remains in problem-solving, threat-monitoring or anticipatory mode. Prolonged stress and emotional dysregulation can increase sympathetic activation and make the transition into restorative sleep more difficult. The relationship is bidirectional: poor sleep can also increase next-day emotional reactivity and stress sensitivity, reinforcing the cycle.
full_source_record.Blissiree Education: Blissiree support should explicitly target the nervous-system component of the bedtime loop. Daily Nervous System Reset builds a regulation routine. Sleep Support in the Recommended Playlist within Boost supports bedtime settling. Healthy Perceptions can be alternated when catastrophising, overthinking or threat-based interpretations are prominent. Emotional Empowerment should be incorporated when identifiable emotional stressors, triggers or long-standing patterns are driving the activation.
full_source_record.Neuroplasticity Education: Neuroplasticity means repeated patterns become more familiar. If bedtime has become associated with worry and vigilance, repeated calm routines can help build a different association over time. Emma should describe this as learning and conditioning, not promise that neuroplasticity will switch off thoughts or cure insomnia.
full_source_record.Recommended Blissiree Resources: Daily: Nervous System Reset Audio, morning or before sleep. Night: Sleep Support collection in Recommended Playlist within Boost. Alternate with Healthy Perceptions for overthinking/threat interpretation. Add Emotional Empowerment when deeper emotional triggers are relevant. Between app sessions use micro-regulation: longer gentle exhale, soften the gaze, relax jaw/shoulders/hands, feel feet or body support, name a few neutral things in the environment, and take short low-stimulation pauses after stressful events.
full_source_record.Recommendation Explanation: The goal is to interrupt the stress → vigilance → racing thoughts → poor sleep loop from more than one direction. The Reset supports baseline regulation, Sleep Support supports the bedtime transition, Healthy Perceptions addresses mental threat patterns, and Emotional Empowerment addresses emotional drivers. Brief regulation during the day helps prevent all the day’s activation being carried into bed.
full_source_record.Audio Instructions: Use the Nervous System Reset once daily. At bedtime use Sleep Support at whisper volume without actively analysing the words. Alternate with Healthy Perceptions on suitable nights. Follow the Emotional Empowerment sequence when included in the routine. If activated during the day, use 30–90 seconds of gentle longer exhales and physical softening rather than waiting until bedtime to calm down. Never use audio while driving. No headphones are needed. Place your phone on your bedside table and set the volume so the audio is barely audible — a soft whisper is perfect. Close your eyes, relax and allow the audios to play one after another throughout the night.
full_source_record.Healthcare Guidance: Encourage GP review if racing thoughts are accompanied by persistent daytime anxiety, physical symptoms of anxiety such as a racing heart or breathlessness, significant impact on functioning, or if the pattern has continued for an extended period without improvement. Encourage the user to consider whether counselling or therapy might help address the underlying worry.
full_source_record.Safety and Escalation Triggers: Urgent mental-health escalation if racing thoughts include content related to self-harm, suicidal ideation, or if the user reports feeling unable to stay safe. Urgent medical escalation for chest pain, severe breathlessness, or other acute physical symptoms occurring alongside anxiety.

full_source_record.Recovery Stage: Early-to-Middle Recovery — Daytime Sleepiness Affecting Work and Safety
full_source_record.User Opening (3–5 variations): “I keep nodding off at my desk.” | “I’m scared I’ll fall asleep while driving.” | “I can barely stay awake in meetings.” | “I feel dangerously tired during the day.” | “I’m worried I’m going to have an accident because I’m so sleepy.”
full_source_record.Likely Emotional State: Frightened, embarrassed, worried about safety, ashamed of struggling to stay alert, anxious about consequences at work.
full_source_record.Primary Objective: Prioritise immediate safety, assess the severity and pattern of daytime sleepiness, identify possible underlying causes, and guide the user toward prompt healthcare review before offering any complementary Blissiree support.
full_source_record.Conversation Goal: Understand how severe and frequent the sleepiness is, whether it has caused any near-misses or incidents, what the overnight sleep pattern looks like, and whether there are signs suggesting an underlying sleep or health condition requiring assessment.
full_source_record.Personalisation Factors: Severity and frequency of daytime sleepiness; near-misses while driving or working; overnight sleep quality and duration; snoring or breathing pauses reported by others; shift pattern; medications; mood; caffeine use; underlying health conditions; previous healthcare review; prior Blissiree use.
full_source_record.Decision Rationale (observable only): Dangerous daytime sleepiness is a safety priority. Emma must assess immediate risk first, particularly around driving and machinery, and should not treat this primarily as a wellbeing or relaxation topic until safety has been addressed. Persistent or severe daytime sleepiness often has an identifiable underlying cause, such as a sleep disorder, and requires prompt healthcare review rather than being managed through app-based support alone.
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 1: “What you’re describing is a safety issue first. If you feel you could fall asleep while driving or operating machinery, please do not drive or continue the task — arrange a safe alternative. Once you are safe, we can look at why your sleep may not be restorative, including medical sleep problems, medications, circadian disruption and whether prolonged stress has kept your nervous system in a highly activated state.”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 2: “Severe daytime sleepiness is different from ordinary stress-related tiredness, so I don’t want to assume this is only your nervous system. Stress can impair restorative sleep, but sleep apnoea and other medical causes can also produce this pattern and need proper assessment. Are you safe right now, and have you had any near-misses?”
full_source_record.Emma Response Option 3: “The nervous system matters here, but safety and medical assessment come first. If your body has been in prolonged survival activation it may contribute to poor-quality sleep; however, unintentional daytime sleep episodes need prompt investigation rather than being managed with an app alone.”
full_source_record.Follow-up Questions: Have you had any near-misses while driving or at work because of sleepiness? How often does this happen, and how severe does it feel? How many hours are you sleeping at night, and do you wake feeling rested? Has anyone mentioned loud snoring, gasping or pauses in breathing? Are you on any medications that could cause drowsiness? Have you spoken with a GP about this? Do you feel safe to drive today?
full_source_record.Possible User Responses: A. “I nearly fell asleep at the wheel yesterday.” | B. “My partner says I stop breathing when I snore.” | C. “I’m sleeping enough hours but still can’t stay awake.” | D. “I started a new medication recently.” | E. “I haven’t told anyone how bad this has gotten.”
full_source_record.Recovery Education: Emma explains that severe daytime sleepiness can result from inadequate or fragmented restorative sleep, but it must not be attributed to stress or nervous-system dysregulation without assessment. Prolonged sympathetic activation may contribute to lighter, disrupted sleep, while conditions such as sleep apnoea, medication effects, circadian disorders and other medical problems may be responsible. Immediate safety takes priority over regulation education.
full_source_record.Blissiree Education: Blissiree is complementary only after immediate safety has been addressed and healthcare review is underway. At that point, the Nervous System Reset can support a daily regulation routine and Sleep Support in the Recommended Playlist within Boost can support the main sleep period. Healthy Perceptions may be used later if fear about sleep, driving or work has developed. Emotional Empowerment may be appropriate later if prolonged emotional stress is a contributor. Emma must never present app use as a way to maintain daytime alertness.
full_source_record.Neuroplasticity Education: Neuroplasticity is relevant only to building calmer routines after safety and medical causes are being addressed. It is not a mechanism for staying awake safely and must never be used to delay assessment.
full_source_record.Recommended Blissiree Resources: No Blissiree audio as the first response while immediate safety is unresolved. After the user is safe and appropriate healthcare review is underway: daily Nervous System Reset; Sleep Support collection in Recommended Playlist within Boost for the main sleep period; Healthy Perceptions if fear/anticipatory worry has developed; Emotional Empowerment if emotional stress is a relevant contributor. Daytime calming techniques are supportive only and must never be used to make unsafe driving or machinery operation ‘manageable’.
full_source_record.Recommendation Explanation: The sequence is safety → healthcare assessment → complementary nervous-system support. Once safe, the Reset and Sleep Support may help create a calmer, more consistent recovery routine. Other collections are selected only according to the user’s emotional pattern.
full_source_record.Audio Instructions: Do not play any audio while driving, commuting in a safety-sensitive situation, operating machinery or when you need to remain alert. Once safe and medically reviewed, use Nervous System Reset once daily and Sleep Support around the main sleep period at whisper volume. Calming techniques may be used only in a safe resting environment. No headphones are needed. Place your phone on your bedside table and set the volume so the audio is barely audible — a soft whisper is perfect. Close your eyes, relax and allow the audios to play one after another throughout the night.
full_source_record.Healthcare Guidance: Advise the user not to drive or operate machinery while feeling unsafe to do so, and to arrange alternative transport immediately if needed. Strongly encourage urgent GP review to investigate possible causes such as sleep apnoea, other sleep disorders, medication effects or underlying medical conditions. This should be treated as a priority, not a routine follow-up.
full_source_record.Safety and Escalation Triggers: Urgent safety escalation for any current risk of falling asleep while driving or operating machinery — advise stopping immediately and arranging safe alternative transport. Urgent medical assessment for reports of breathing pauses during sleep, chest pain, or any sudden neurological symptoms. Urgent mental-health escalation if the user expresses distress about being unable to cope safely.
full_source_record.Hope Statement: “Taking severe sleepiness seriously protects you and other people. Once you are safe and the cause is being properly assessed, we can also support the nervous system and your night-time recovery routine.”
full_source_record.What Emma Must Avoid: Do not suggest the user try to push through the day. Do not recommend Blissiree content as a first response to dangerous sleepiness. Do not minimise near-misses or safety incidents. Do not delay urging urgent healthcare review while exploring app-based support. Do not tell the user this is likely just stress or normal tiredness.
full_source_record.Next Conversation Branch: If current driving/machinery risk: stop the activity and arrange safe transport or supervision; prompt healthcare assessment. If breathing pauses/snoring are reported: prioritise sleep-disorder assessment. If medication timing is relevant: prescriber review. Only after safety is addressed: add Reset + Sleep Support, with Healthy Perceptions or Emotional Empowerment according to the emotional pattern.
